clue.text: Obtuseness of the barmaid ?

parts.note: Hebe was cupbearer who poured nectar for the gods, a heavenly barmaid; the word for dullness of mind looks as if it were built on her name

explanation.surface: A complaint about a slow-witted woman serving behind the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: Hebe, Greek goddess of youth, served the gods their drinks, so she is 'the barmaid'; the answer, meaning mental dullness, starts with her name as though it were her own quality.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a rare literary term for mental dullness or lethargy, a synonym of obtuseness.

clue.text: He hawks, not to say rooks

definitions.meaning: a pedlar who sells goods noisily in the street
rooks means cheats or swindles, the sort of thing a sharp salesman does

explanation.definitionFit: A street pedlar is the man who cries his wares, and the same word describes a cheating sharp operator who swindles buyers.

clue.text: Sounds rather on the dotty side the prince — behaved so

indicators.note: Sounds tells the solver the phrase is to be heard, not spelt

parts.note: a little dotty is barmy, and on that side gives side: barmy side

explanation.surface: A prince is said to have acted in a rather crazy manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounds' turns 'barmy side' into the name of the Barmecide prince of the Arabian Nights, who served a beggar an imaginary feast, which is the dotty behaviour of 'behaved so'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Arabian Nights a nobleman of the Barmecide family hosts a pretend banquet of empty dishes for a hungry beggar.

clue.text: Don't mention it: we understand

parts.note: something agreed without being spoken aloud is understood silently

explanation.surface: A polite brush-off after an apology.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don't mention it' is usually a reply to thanks; here it means the thing is never said, yet still understood.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacit means implied or understood without being stated.

clue.text: Get your tail down ?

parts.note: a garment's trailing hem made wet and muddy by trailing along the ground

explanation.surface: An order to a dog to stop wagging.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an animal lowering its tail; the answer means to soil a long skirt or coat-tail by trailing it through mud.
explanation.definitionFit: To draggle is to make something wet and dirty by trailing it along the ground.

clue.text: Pater's fed up with it

indicators.note: fed up suggests the letters have been upset and stirred into a new order

parts.note: the word is used letter for letter, its S included

explanation.surface: Father has had enough of something and says so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fed up' signals rearranging the letters of PATERS; read as a whole, the clue also describes a meal, which is what one is fed with.
explanation.definitionFit: A repast is a meal, the thing one is fed with.

clue.text: Industrial city come to a bad end — is it necessary ?

parts.note: Essen is the steel-making city of the Ruhr in Germany

indicators.note: bad here means spoiled, so the word for the end is mangled into a new order

parts.note: a tail is the end of something

explanation.surface: Must a manufacturing town meet a sorry fate?
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' signals the rearrangement of the word for end; 'Industrial city' is Essen in the Ruhr, and 'come to a' and 'is it' are only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Something essential is indispensable, absolutely required.

clue.text: "Thou craggy ocean pyramid " (Keats)

parts.note: the opening line of a Keats sonnet addressed to a rocky island in the Firth of Clyde

explanation.surface: A quotation from a Romantic poet about a peak in the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats's sonnet 'To Ailsa Rock' opens 'Hearken, thou craggy ocean pyramid!'; Ailsa Craig is a granite islet off the Scottish coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Ailsa Craig, the Ailsa Rock of the poem, is a steep granite island shaped like a pyramid rising from the sea.

clue.text: Bert I'm done up in cords

indicators.note: done up means fixed or reassembled, so the letters are put together in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A man named Bert gets dressed smartly in corduroy trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'done up' rearranges BERT IM; 'cords' looks like corduroys but is the measure of cut wood.
explanation.definitionFit: A cord is a measure of cut wood for fuel, so cords are stacks of logs.

clue.text: Sam Dowser ?

parts.note: a dowser finds wells with a divining rod, so is a well-finder; Sam is Mr Pickwick's servant in Dickens

explanation.surface: A man called Sam who divines for water.
explanation.walkthrough: A dowser searches for wells, so could be called a 'well-er'; Sam Weller is Mr Pickwick's Cockney manservant in Dickens's Pickwick Papers.
explanation.definitionFit: Sam Weller is the shrewd manservant in The Pickwick Papers.

clue.text: Foot-trouble, note, makes the roué rail

parts.note: a corn is a painful patch of hard skin on the foot
C is a musical note
a roué is a debauched man, a rake

explanation.surface: A man with sore feet and a letter in hand makes a womaniser complain bitterly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rail' looks like a verb, to complain; it is the bird family, and 'makes' simply joins the pieces to it.
explanation.definitionFit: The corncrake is a bird of the rail family, found in meadows and hayfields.

clue.text: School House for David Copperfield

parts.note: in Dickens's novel the boy is sent to a boarding school run by Mr Creakle; the clue asks for the name of that establishment

explanation.surface: Which boarding house did Dickens's young hero belong to at school?
explanation.walkthrough: In David Copperfield the hero is sent to Salem House, Mr Creakle's harsh school near London; 'House' is part of its name, not a dormitory division.
explanation.definitionFit: Salem House is the school David attends in Dickens's novel, so its first word answers the question.

clue.text: What a way to treat pore labourers!

definitions.text: What a way to treat pore labourers!

parts.words: What a way to treat pore labourers!
parts.note: read as poor labourers, it is overworking employees for little pay; read with skin pores, it is what pores do when the body is hot

explanation.surface: An outcry at the exploitation of underpaid workers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pore' stands in for 'poor': exploiting cheap workers is to make them toil in a sweatshop, while the tiny openings in skin do the same thing when hot.
explanation.definitionFit: To overwork employees for low wages is to make them toil hard, and skin pores give out moisture in the same word.

clue.text: Storm-tossed girl ? She's rooted to the ground

parts.note: gal is an informal word for a girl
something tossed in a storm is caught in a high wind: in gale

explanation.surface: A young woman caught in bad weather finds herself stuck fast to the spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Storm-tossed girl' means a girl caught in a gale: GAL, then IN GALE. 'She' is a plant, a sedge, which is literally rooted in the soil.
explanation.definitionFit: Galingale is a sedge, a plant with aromatic roots growing in damp soil, so it is fixed in the earth.

clue.text: One of those expressing thistly preferences to Susie ?

definitions.text: One of those expressing thistly preferences to Susie ?

parts.words: One of those expressing thistly preferences to Susie ?
parts.note: a letter sent to a woman, read by a lisper who turns every S into a TH sound, as the clue's thistly spelling mimics

explanation.surface: Someone writes to a girlfriend about a fondness for prickly plants.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue mimics a lisp: 'thistly' is 'thisly' said with a lisp, and a lisper would say the answer as 'e-pithle'. The answer is a letter, the kind of thing one sends to Susie.
explanation.definitionFit: An epistle is a formal or literary word for a letter, such as one written to a friend.

clue.text: Journeys end in lovers meeting — notedly long one in this case

definitions.text: Journeys end in lovers meeting — notedly long one in this case

parts.words: Journeys end in lovers meeting — notedly long one in this case
parts.note: a line from Twelfth Night, plus a hint at the First World War marching song about a long way to an Irish town where a sweetheart waits

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare quotation about lovers reunited after travel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Journeys end in lovers meeting' is Feste's song in Twelfth Night; the famous song says 'It's a long way to Tipperary', where the singer's sweetheart lives, and 'notedly' means as the music has it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish town of the soldiers' song is where the singer's sweetheart lives, at the end of a long journey.

clue.text: Opera in Edinburgh — what weather there !

annotationWithheld.why: Opera in Edinburgh — what weather there ! (6): the answer runs across 'operA IN EDinburgh', so 'in' is both part of the hidden run and the only possible hiding indicator; a word doing two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: Opera in Edinburgh — what weather there !

clue.text: Presented with a cauliflower?

parts.note: a boxer's ear swollen and deformed by blows is called a cauliflower ear, so receiving one leaves a mark on that ear

explanation.surface: Someone receives a vegetable as a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'cauliflower ear' is a boxer's battered ear; given one, you have been literally marked on the ear. The usual sense is set aside for a purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: Earmarked normally means set aside for a purpose, from the marks cut in livestock's ears; here the ear is marked by a punch.

clue.text: Rung up, one may be who has

definitions.text: Rung up, one may be who has

parts.words: Rung up, one may be who has
parts.note: climbing a ladder rung by rung takes a person higher, so someone who has gone up that way may be said to be rung up

explanation.surface: A telephone call that someone has made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rung up' reads as telephoned; it means having gone up a ladder rung by rung, which is what someone who has climbed has done.
explanation.definitionFit: To have climbed or gone up is the meaning of the past tense of the verb.

clue.text: Ring for the man in charge

definitions.meaning: a guard ring worn to stop a more valuable ring slipping off the finger
a custodian or warden responsible for a place or animals

explanation.definitionFit: A guard ring holding another in place shares the name with a warden, someone who looks after a place or animals.

clue.text: Herb, you're such a green policeman !

definitions.text: Herb, you're such a green policeman !

parts.words: Herb, you're such a green policeman !
parts.note: herb ... is a wild geranium, a green plant; the first name of Sir ... Peel gave a slang word for a police officer

explanation.surface: Someone teases a raw young constable named Herb.
explanation.walkthrough: Herb Robert is a common wild geranium; 'robert' was old British slang for a policeman, from Sir Robert Peel, founder of the Metropolitan Police. 'green' means both plant-like and inexperienced.
explanation.definitionFit: Herb Robert is a wild plant, and the same name is old slang for a constable after Sir Robert Peel.

clue.text: Master, a cut-back in weaponry

indicators.note: back, joined to cut, tells the solver the whole run of pieces is read backwards

parts.note: sir is the title for a master or a schoolmaster
to lop is to cut off

explanation.surface: A military commander orders a reduction in arms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut-back' looks like an arms reduction, but 'back' is the instruction to read every piece in reverse as one run; 'in weaponry' defines a nuclear missile.
explanation.definitionFit: Polaris was the submarine-launched nuclear missile of the British and American arsenals, a piece of military hardware.

clue.text: Dame Feathers

parts.note: a feathered lady, the name given to the hen in Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale and in old fable

explanation.surface: A grand lady known for her plumage.
explanation.walkthrough: Dame Partlet is the hen, wife of the cockerel Chanticleer, in Chaucer and in Reynard the Fox; she is a dame dressed in feathers.
explanation.definitionFit: Partlet is the traditional name for a hen in English fable, a feathered matron.

clue.text: Meet points that are raised in this regard

indicators.note: in a down clue raised means lifted upward, so the run of pieces is read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
S and E are compass points, south and east

explanation.surface: A get-together where certain issues are raised in this respect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns MEET plus SE upwards as one run, as befits a down clue; 'in this' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To esteem someone is to hold them in high regard, and the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: August following

parts.note: the calendar month that comes straight after the eighth month of the year

explanation.surface: A dignified retinue trailing behind someone grand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'August' looks like the adjective meaning dignified, with 'following' as a band of admirers; it is the month, and the answer is the one after it.
explanation.definitionFit: The ninth month of the year comes immediately after the eighth, so it follows in the calendar.

clue.text: Ah, lip, the bottle

annotationWithheld.why: Ah, lip, the bottle (5): the answer is the letters of AH LIP rearranged, but no clue word signals the anagram (the scan prints the clue this way)

clue.text: Would a sound churching reform him?

definitions.text: Would a sound churching reform him?

parts.words: Would a sound churching reform him?
parts.note: the rogue's name is said exactly like the main body of a church, so a good dose of church might set such a rascal right

explanation.surface: Would regular attendance at services straighten out a scoundrel?
explanation.walkthrough: The rascal sounds just like the nave of a church, so a 'sound churching' plays on both a thorough dose of religion and the identical sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A knave is a dishonest rogue, the kind of man a moral reform is aimed at.

clue.text: Look sharp, Mack !

parts.note: Mack the gangster of The Threepenny Opera carries a blade, and the song about him gave him that nickname

explanation.surface: Someone tells a man named Mack to hurry up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look sharp' means hurry up; it hints at the blade of Macheath, Mack the Knife of Brecht and Weill's Threepenny Opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Mack the Knife is the song nickname of Macheath, and a blade is a sharp cutting tool.

clue.text: Pronouncedly gory her society debut

parts.note: in Shaw's Pygmalion the flower girl, at her first polite tea party, startles everyone by saying 'Not bloody likely', a gory word spoken aloud

explanation.surface: A young woman's first appearance in high society goes horribly wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shaw's Pygmalion, the Cockney flower girl Doolittle makes her society debut and shocks the room with 'Not bloody likely'; 'gory' is 'bloody', and 'Pronouncedly' because she said it aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliza Doolittle is the heroine of Pygmalion whose first society outing ends with her famous swear word.

clue.text: Made whoopee, but Lor', was brought back and beaten

indicators.note: brought back tells the solver to read the exclamation from end to start

parts.note: taken as written, an old exclamation for Lord
licked means beaten or thrashed

explanation.surface: Someone who had been partying is dragged home and given a thrashing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lor'' is an old exclamation for Lord; 'brought back' is the reversal instruction, and 'was' and 'and' are links. 'Made whoopee' means partied noisily.
explanation.definitionFit: To make whoopee is to celebrate boisterously, which is what frolicking high spirits amount to.

clue.text: Feeling nohow, these nationals ?

parts.note: a vague sense of being unwell, a French-borrowed word, is said the same way as the people of a South-East Asian nation

explanation.surface: Do people from a certain country all feel out of sorts?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feeling nohow' (old slang for out of sorts) is malaise, which sounds just like the plural of the people of Malaysia.
explanation.definitionFit: Malays are the people native to the Malay Peninsula, citizens of Malaysia and nearby lands.

clue.text: Gathered no wool

parts.note: wool-gathering means daydreaming, so one who did no wool-gathering paid heed

explanation.surface: A shepherd collected no fleece at all this year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wool-gathering' is daydreaming; someone who did none was paying attention. 'Gathered' also hints at people assembling, as at a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: To have paid heed, or to have been present at an event, both fit the past tense of the verb.
